items.anchor_quote: In both cases the alarm boundary is indicated with a dashed red line.
items.summary: Origin of the 2.0 V level: Meyer et al. 2018 Figure 9 plots ISS (right) and Space Shuttle (left) detector signal versus particle number concentration with a dashed 'Detector alarm boundary'. The numeric value is not written in the text; visual inspection of the figure shows the ISS boundary on the 2.0 V gridline (axis 0-7 V) and the Shuttle (STS) boundary slightly above 0.4 V. Within the examined SAME (PSI-102) and SAME-R (PSI-101) final-report texts, including their appended papers, no 2.0 V or other ISS scatter-voltage alarm threshold is stated (searched for 2 V / 2.0 V / alarm / threshold / volt patterns).

items.location: Background section on ISS and STS detectors (report body)
items.anchor_quote: detector was designed to alarm at 1% obscuration per foot using an Underwriters Laboratory
items.summary: The SAME final report gives the ISS smoke detector's design alarm criterion as 1% obscuration per foot in a UL smoke box (and the STS detector's as a mass concentration of 2 mg/m3 for 5 s, based on 1 micron particles). This is a specification in obscuration units, not a voltage on the recorded scatter channel.

items.anchor_quote: The data points below the voltage threshold boundaries are cases where the detectors would
items.summary: Meyer et al. interpret Figure 9 points below the voltage boundary as cases where the detectors would have failed to alarm: for the Space Shuttle detector Kapton, Teflon and lamp wick; for the ISS detector Kapton and Teflon. The ISS detector would not have alarmed for over half of the Kapton tests and about two thirds of the Teflon tests; the Shuttle detector, though somewhat less sensitive overall, did better than the ISS detector on Teflon smoke under the tested conditions.

items.anchor_quote: The ISS detector would not have alarmed for over half of the Kapton smoke
items.summary: Comparison of Meyer's aggregate statement with Model C counts: Kapton primary runs below 2 V = 12/21 (0.571; all records incl. secondary 21/36 = 0.583) - consistent with 'over half'. Teflon below 2 V = 11/15 primary (0.733), 7/11 SAME-R primary (0.636), 18/23 all records (0.783) - near the stated 2/3 but not exactly reproducible because the paper does not state which points (campaign, primary/secondary, P-Trak availability) are plotted.
items.scope_notes: Directionally consistent; exact denominator mismatch unresolved. Do not use Meyer's fractions as Model C accuracy targets.

items.anchor_quote: Since the ISS smoke detector is calibrated with 0.6 μm particles and the laser
items.summary: Meyer et al. explain the ISS shortfall physically: the ISS detector is calibrated with 0.6 um particles and its laser wavelength is about 1 um, so response is expected to drop for particles much smaller than that; Kapton smoke had TEM diameters of average mass below 0.3 um. They flag this as a concern because Kapton and Teflon are common in spacecraft electrical systems and may be among the first materials to overheat.

items.location: Section C.1 Moment Instrument Results, Table 1 (row Teflon / Unaged); also external/model_c/data/references/20130000422.txt line 491 (layout text)
items.anchor_quote: Table 1: Diameter results for baseline runs for each material (Diameters are in micrometers).
items.summary: NTRS 20130000422 (Urban et al., 'Particle Morphology and Size Results from the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment-2', 42nd ICES, AIAA 2012-3536, July 2012) Table 1 prints for unaged Teflon: geometric mean 0.081 um, count mean 0.101 um, diameter of average mass 0.170 um, sigma_g 2.198. Applying the lognormal (Hatch-Choate) relations used in Model C train.py (count = Dg exp(0.5 ln^2 sg), mass = Dg exp(1.5 ln^2 sg)) gives count 0.110450 um and mass 0.205367 um. With +/-0.0005 rounding on Dg and sg the recomputed ranges are 0.109749-0.111152 and 0.203989-0.206745 um, disjoint from the printed 0.1005-0.1015 and 0.1695-0.1705. Conversely the printed count/mass pair implies sigma_g 2.0577 and Dg 0.0778 um. The other 9 rows are consistent within rounding.

conditions.gravity: low gravity, ISS Microgravity Science Glovebox (flight)

items.scope_notes: Algebraic consistency check of published rounded values, not new measurements; independent of the ISS 2 V labels. Matches Model C's external_checks.csv and teflon_table1_check.json to all printed digits.

items.anchor_quote: source_internal_inconsistency_unresolved
items.summary: Model C recorded the same unaged-Teflon discrepancy (recomputed count 0.11045 um, mass 0.20537 um; implied sigma_g 2.0577, Dg 0.07785 um) and left it unresolved, stating that no column-averaging explanation is documented in the publication; its 9 other Table 1 rows are 'consistent_with_source_rounding'. This agent's independent recomputation reproduces those numbers exactly.
items.scope_notes: Agreement between Model C and this audit; see next item for a workbook-level explanation candidate.

items.location: sheet 'Teflon R&T plots' cells BR28, BS28, BU28, BV28 (row label 'Baseline Aging') -> sheet 'ICES 2012 Paper data table' E12:I12, M25:P25 and ROUND(...,3) cells M9:P9
items.anchor_quote: =AVERAGE(BR10:BR11,BR15:BR16)
items.summary: Workbook trace of the unaged-Teflon row: the PSI workbook sheet 'ICES 2012 Paper data table' rounds to 3 decimals exactly the printed Table 1 values (0.081, 0.101, 0.17, 2.198); they come from 'Teflon R&T plots' row 28, where count mean, mass diameter, sigma_g and Dg are each a separate AVERAGE over four SAME-R baseline runs (56/T02, 58/T03, 79/T04, 89/T08). Each run satisfies the lognormal relations exactly, but the runs are heterogeneous (sigma_g 1.511-2.764, Dg 0.0317-0.1495 um), so applying the relations to the averaged Dg (0.081475) and sigma_g (2.198322) gives 0.1111/0.2066 um instead of the averaged 0.1007/0.1696 um. Column-wise averaging of lognormal parameters is therefore a documented-in-workbook mechanism that reproduces the inconsistency.

Its PDF p4 gives the P-Trak range (0 to 10^5 particles/cm3, 20 nm to 1 um) and DustTrak range (0.001 to 100 mg/m3), matching what Model C cites; the only 'saturated' wording on pp4-5 refers to the P-Trak isopropanol vapour, so ISS-signal saturation is supported by Meyer et al. 2018 section 3.2, not by this paper.

items.location: external/model_c/STATUS.json known_limits[0]; MODEL_CARD.md line 7; domain.json key target
items.anchor_quote: Experimental2V proxy, not reported operational alarm
items.summary: Model C's target is a derived experimental proxy (recorded ISS scatter >= 2 V), not a reported operational alarm, alarm event or safety certification; Agent 5 must phrase any Model C output as 'signal reached the 2 V reference level in the experiment', never as 'the detector alarmed'.
items.scope_notes: Applies to all Model C labels and predictions.

items.anchor_quote: Material identity explains the headline score
items.summary: Material identity explains Model C's score: a per-material majority baseline reaches balanced accuracy 0.891342 +/- 0.048823 on the saved outer folds, a fixed forest 0.900433 +/- 0.056572, and the original nested-selection headline 0.870152 +/- 0.076360. Forest minus material-majority is 0.009091 +/- 0.020328 with 4 of 5 fold differences exactly zero, so controlled conditions add no demonstrated predictive value beyond material.
items.scope_notes: Post-hoc comparison on the same outer groups; fold SD is not a confidence interval. The 0.5 'majority baseline' in the original headline is a global-majority baseline, not the material baseline.

items.location: external/model_c/reports/metrics.json per_material.Kapton.recall and per_material.Teflon.recall; evaluation.md Per material table
items.summary: On held-out (nested out-of-fold) predictions Model C recovers almost none of the Kapton and Teflon runs that reached 2 V: Kapton recall 0.111 (1 of 9 positives; confusion [[11,1],[8,1]]), Teflon recall 0.0 (0 of 4; [[11,0],[4,0]]), balanced accuracy 0.514 and 0.5. It effectively predicts 'below 2 V' for these materials.
items.scope_notes: Kapton 19 + Teflon 15 groups. Model C cannot be used to identify which Kapton/Teflon conditions reach 2 V.

items.anchor_quote: Post-hoc within-material diagnostic; fixed C1 balanced logistic; no model export or deployment claim
items.summary: Within-material logistic diagnostics on numeric controls only: Kapton pooled out-of-fold balanced accuracy 0.583 (recall 0.333; fold values 0.375, 1.0, 0.35), Teflon 0.739 (recall 0.75; one fold single-class). They are small, post-hoc, unserialized and confounded by test matrix, campaign and reused samples.
items.scope_notes: Not evidence of reliable condition effects; scatter relationships are descriptive, not causal.

items.anchor_quote: Maximum same-material standardized nearest condition distance from a different training group
items.summary: Model C's out-of-distribution flag is a heuristic: a request is flagged when its standardized nearest-neighbour distance to same-material training conditions exceeds 9.32 (the largest such distance between different training groups). Range checks use global ranges, so a Kapton request at Rt/R0 1.22 (Kapton was only tested at 1.38-1.48) with 0 cm/s, 10 s heating, 1 s aging is accepted, predicted True and only flagged OOD (distance 10.03).
items.scope_notes: OOD flag is not a calibrated uncertainty; unseen materials are rejected, but unseen per-material condition combinations are only flagged.

items.location: external/model_c/reports/evaluation.md lines 48-55 (Campaign shift; leave-one-material-out); metrics.json leave_one_material_out_stress_test
items.anchor_quote: Inference rejects unseen materials; this diagnostic does not support deployment on held-out materials.
items.summary: Generalization stress tests are weak: training on SAME and testing on SAME-R gives balanced accuracy 0.629 (12 Pyrell rows excluded as unseen), SAME-R to SAME 0.846 on 17 rows; leave-one-material-out logistic gives Kapton 0.458 and Teflon 0.443. Model C rejects unseen materials.
items.scope_notes: No support for other materials, campaigns or hardware.

items.anchor_quote: No ambient spacecraft generalization, time-to-alarm, flame/fatality risk, detector certification, or unseen-material prediction.
items.summary: Model C's stated scope excludes ambient spacecraft generalization, time-to-alarm, flame or fatality risk, detector certification and unseen materials; it also notes only 84 primary records with uneven coverage, unresolved per-row saturation/LOD, blank (unknown) SAME-R quality flags, Rt/R0 not determining sample temperature, and no raw instrument calibration reconstruction.
items.scope_notes: Agent 5 must not extend Model C outputs to flaming fires, full-scale cabins or alarm timing.

items.anchor_quote: No uncertainty interval or calibrated probability is claimed.
items.summary: Model C reports no uncertainty intervals and no calibrated probabilities; fold standard deviations describe variability only.
items.scope_notes: Any probability-like number shown by Agent 5 from Model C would be unsupported.

items.anchor_quote: These describe the available primary experiments, not probabilities for new fires.
items.summary: The measured fractions (Kapton 9/21, Teflon 4/15, Lampwick 17/17, Pyrell 12/12, Silicone 19/19 reaching 2 V) describe the available primary experiments, not probabilities for new fires.
items.scope_notes: Use as test-matrix description with group counts, never as detection probability.

items.anchor_quote: SAME-R source quality flags are blank/unknown.
items.summary: SAME's fan-problem and flat-profile flags are 'n' but SAME-R's are blank, which Model C treats as unknown rather than verified absence; together with author-reduced (not re-calibrated) channels this limits data-quality filtering for the SAME-R runs that hold most below-2 V cases.
items.scope_notes: Quality of individual SAME-R runs cannot be confirmed from the workbook flags.

Which tests/points underlie Meyer's 'over half of the Kapton' and '2/3 of the Teflon' ISS non-alarm fractions (campaign, primary vs secondary, P-Trak availability)? Model C counts are near but not identical.
